mcq.prompt: Which of these is NOT an object type?
mcq.explain: An object type describes a region of storage that can hold a value. References, functions and void are not object types — which is why sizeof(f) is ill-formed for a function f. Pointers to functions, on the other hand, are ordinary object types.

mcq.prompt: Two structs are declared with identical members and identical layout, under different names. What does C++'s type system say about them?
choices: They are the same type, because C++ is structurally typed
They are distinct types, because C++ is nominally typed
They are the same type only if both are trivially copyable
They are distinct types only if they have different alignment
mcq.explain: C++ is nominally typed: separately declared class or enumeration types stay distinct even when their representations match. Structural typing (same shape means same type) is what languages like TypeScript do.

mcq.section: Fundamental types, fixed-width integers, and literals
mcq.prompt: You are serialising a field to a wire protocol that specifies a 64-bit signed integer. Which declaration states that requirement?
mcq.explain: std::int64_t states the representation directly. long is 8 bytes on LP64 Linux/macOS but 4 bytes on LLP64 Windows, so it serialises a different amount of data per platform; long long happens to be 64-bit on both but still only promises a minimum range.

mcq.section: Fundamental types, fixed-width integers, and literals
mcq.prompt: What is the type of the literal 4.2 in `double rate = 4.2;`?
choices: It depends on the type being initialised
mcq.explain: An unsuffixed floating literal is a double; 4.2f would be a float. The spelling of a literal fixes its type before any surrounding conversion — the destination type never reaches back and changes it.

mcq.section: Fundamental types, fixed-width integers, and literals
mcq.prompt: What is the type of the string literal "a"?
mcq.explain: A string literal is an array of const char including the terminating '\0', so "a" is const char[2]. It decays to const char* in most expressions, which is why the pointer answer is tempting — but decay is a conversion applied to the array, not the literal's own type.

mcq.prompt: Given `int* const fixed = &bid;`, which statement is legal?
mcq.explain: Read the declaration from the identifier outward: fixed is a const pointer to a (non-const) int. The pointee is writable, the pointer is not. `const int* observed` is the other way round.

mcq.prompt: `const_cast` is used to remove const from a pointer to an object that was itself declared const, and the result is written through. What happens?
choices: The write silently has no effect
The write is fine — const is only a compile-time check
The program is ill-formed and will not compile
mcq.explain: const_cast makes the write compile, but writing to an object that was created const is undefined behaviour — the implementation may have placed it in read-only storage or propagated its value. Casting away const is only safe when the underlying object was not const to begin with.

mcq.prompt: What does `volatile` guarantee?
choices: That the value is re-read from main memory rather than cache
That accesses are ordered with respect to other threads
That each access through the volatile path is an observable side effect the compiler may not elide
mcq.explain: volatile only stops the compiler eliding or coalescing accesses; its real use is memory-mapped device registers. It supplies neither atomicity nor inter-thread ordering — those come from the memory model and std::atomic.

mcq.prompt: `int& price = bid;` followed by `price = ask;` does what?
choices: Fails to compile because references cannot be assigned
Creates a copy of ask named price
Rebinds price to refer to ask
mcq.explain: A reference is bound once and never reseated. Assignment through a reference assigns to the referred-to object, so bid receives ask's value. Nothing in the language can make price alias a different object afterwards.

mcq.prompt: A function returns `const std::string&` referring to a std::string local variable. What is the defect?
choices: The returned reference dangles as soon as the function returns
It fails to compile because a const reference cannot bind to a local
The local's lifetime is extended to match the reference
mcq.explain: A returned reference does not carry the referred object's lifetime with it. Lifetime extension applies to binding a temporary to a local const reference, not to returning a reference to a local that is about to be destroyed.

mcq.prompt: Inside `void inspect(int values[10])`, what does `sizeof(values)` evaluate to?
choices: It is ill-formed — you cannot take sizeof an array parameter
mcq.explain: The parameter int values[10] is adjusted to int* values; the 10 documents an intention and enforces nothing. The function will happily accept an array of five elements or a nullptr.

mcq.prompt: What does indexing a built-in array out of bounds do?
choices: Is implementation-defined but always safe under AddressSanitizer
Is undefined behaviour, with no check performed
mcq.explain: Built-in indexing performs no bounds check and throws nothing. AddressSanitizer catches many such accesses in test builds, but detecting undefined behaviour is not the same as making it defined.

mcq.prompt: Which is true of `enum class Side : std::uint8_t { Buy = 1, Sell = 2 };` but NOT of the equivalent unscoped enum?
choices: Its enumerator names do not leak into the surrounding scope
It can have a fixed underlying type
Its values can be compared with ==
Its enumerators can be given explicit values
mcq.explain: Scoping the names and refusing implicit conversion to integer are the two things enum class adds. An unscoped enum may also be given an explicit underlying type and explicit enumerator values.

mcq.prompt: A uint8_t read off the wire holds 7. It is static_cast to `enum class Side : std::uint8_t { Buy = 1, Sell = 2 }`. What is the result?
choices: Undefined behaviour, because no enumerator has the value 7
A valid Side object holding 7; domain validation is still your job
The value is clamped to the nearest enumerator
mcq.explain: Because the underlying type is fixed, every value representable in uint8_t is a valid value of the enumeration, so the cast is well-defined. Undefined behaviour would arise for an enumeration *without* a fixed underlying type. A fixed underlying type solves the representation problem, not the validation problem.

mcq.prompt: Is plain `char` signed or unsigned?
choices: Implementation-defined, and it is a third type distinct from both signed char and unsigned char
Signed, but only when it stores a value above 127
mcq.explain: Plain char is a distinct type from both signed char and unsigned char, and its signedness in integer conversions is implementation-defined — commonly signed on x86 and unsigned on many Arm targets. Use std::int8_t or std::uint8_t when the sign matters.

mcq.prompt: Why prefer std::byte over unsigned char for raw wire storage?
choices: It is guaranteed to be aligned to 8 bytes
It is smaller than unsigned char
It supports arithmetic operators that unsigned char does not
It offers bitwise operations without the accidental arithmetic and signedness of character types
mcq.explain: std::byte models raw memory: bitwise operators work, but `flags + std::byte{1}` does not compile. That removes a class of bugs where a byte silently promotes and takes part in arithmetic.

mcq.prompt: `std::int32_t ticks = 103.875;` — what is stored in ticks?
mcq.explain: Floating-to-integer conversion discards the fractional part, truncating toward zero — it never rounds. This is exactly how a price just below the next tick becomes an off-by-one-tick order.

mcq.prompt: Given overloads `void route(int)` and `void route(int*)`, what do route(0) and route(nullptr) select?
choices: route(0) calls route(int); route(nullptr) calls route(int*)
mcq.explain: The literal 0 is an int (and a legacy null pointer constant), so the int overload is the exact match. nullptr has its own type, std::nullptr_t, which converts to a pointer but not to int — which is precisely why nullptr exists.

mcq.section: Promotions and the usual arithmetic conversions
mcq.prompt: On a typical LP64 system, what is the type of `bid + ask` where both are std::uint8_t?
mcq.explain: Integer promotion converts operands narrower than int to int when int can hold every value of the source type — which it can for uint8_t. Narrow types save storage and cache footprint; they do not make the ALU do narrow arithmetic.

mcq.section: Promotions and the usual arithmetic conversions
mcq.prompt: Why does `-1 > 0u` evaluate to true?
choices: Because 0u is promoted to int, and -1 > 0 is folded to true
Because the compiler evaluates the comparison in long
Because comparison of a negative number with an unsigned is undefined behaviour
Because both operands have the rank of int, so the signed operand converts to unsigned and -1 becomes UINT_MAX
mcq.explain: The usual arithmetic conversions reach the rule where the unsigned type has rank at least as high as the signed type, so the signed operand converts to unsigned int. -1 becomes UINT_MAX, which is greater than 0. Nothing here is undefined — it is well-defined and wrong.

mcq.prompt: Which is true about integer overflow?
choices: Signed overflow is undefined behaviour; unsigned overflow wraps modulo 2^N
Signed overflow wraps; unsigned overflow is undefined behaviour
Both signed and unsigned overflow wrap modulo 2^N
mcq.explain: Unsigned arithmetic is defined modulo 2^N. Signed overflow is undefined behaviour — which is what lets the optimiser assume signed induction variables never wrap and thereby prove trip counts and vectorise.

mcq.prompt: `for (unsigned i = values.size() - 1; i >= 0; --i)` over a std::vector. What is wrong with it?
choices: Only the loop condition: i >= 0 is always true for an unsigned i
Both: the condition can never be false, and an empty vector wraps the initial value
Nothing — it is correct but triggers a -Wsign-compare warning
Only the empty-vector case: size() - 1 wraps to a huge value
mcq.explain: Two independent defects. An unsigned i is never negative, so i >= 0 is always true and decrementing zero wraps to the maximum. Separately, on an empty vector size() - 1 is already SIZE_MAX before the loop starts. Write `for (auto i = values.size(); i-- > 0;)` or use std::ssize.

mcq.prompt: What does `nan == nan` evaluate to, and what does `nan != nan` evaluate to?
mcq.explain: Every ordered comparison with NaN (<, >, <=, >=, ==) is false; != is true. That makes x != x a NaN test, though std::isnan(x) states the intent. It also means a limit check written only as `if (price > maximum) return false;` lets a NaN price straight through.

mcq.prompt: An optimised build compiles `bool valid(double x) { return !std::isnan(x); }` down to an unconditional `return true`. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The function being inlined into a caller that already checked
A compiler bug in the standard library header
mcq.explain: -ffinite-math-only (usually pulled in by -ffast-math) licenses the compiler to assume inputs and results are finite, so the NaN test is provably false and gets deleted. FTZ/DAZ changes subnormals to zero, which is a different hazard and does not touch NaN checks. Never apply fast-math to code that validates prices, limits, or risk.

mcq.prompt: Given `const std::string& view = symbol;`, what type does `auto copy = view;` deduce?
mcq.explain: Plain auto drops top-level const and reference qualifiers, so this silently makes a copy. Write `const auto&` when you meant to alias — that is the deduction form that preserves both.

mcq.prompt: For `const int quantity = 10;`, what are decltype(quantity) and decltype((quantity))?
mcq.explain: For an unparenthesised name, decltype reports the declared type: const int. Parenthesising makes it an lvalue *expression*, and decltype of an lvalue expression of type T is T&, so const int&. This is the trap that makes `decltype(auto) f() { return (local); }` return a dangling reference.

mcq.prompt: Which cast should convert a std::uint8_t read off the wire into a scoped enumeration with that underlying type?
mcq.explain: static_cast performs conversions the type system already permits, including enumeration conversions. reinterpret_cast is for representation reinterpretation at ABI or wire boundaries; dynamic_cast requires a polymorphic source class.

mcq.prompt: Why prefer a named cast over a C-style cast `(T)x`?
choices: A C-style cast is ill-formed in C++23
Only named casts can convert between numeric types
The named casts are faster at runtime
A named cast narrows the permission requested and is greppable in review
mcq.explain: A C-style cast tries combinations of static_cast, const_cast and reinterpret_cast and silently uses whichever works, so it may cast away const when the author only meant a numeric conversion. Named casts carry no extra runtime cost — they cost the conversion requested and nothing more.

mcq.prompt: How many bits of significand precision does a normal binary64 double have?
mcq.explain: 52 bits of fraction are stored, plus the implicit leading 1 that normal values carry, giving 53 bits of precision. Binary32 float stores 23 and so has 24. Subnormals give this up: they use a leading zero instead, trading precision for gradual underflow.

mcq.prompt: For application counts and differences whose valid domain is nonnegative, which type should you reach for by default?
choices: A signed type such as std::int64_t
auto, deduced from whatever the container returns
unsigned, because the domain is nonnegative
mcq.explain: Subtraction is the decisive trap: with unsigned types, `received - expected` becomes a huge positive value when received < expected, silently and without a branch. Reserve unsigned for bit manipulation, modulo arithmetic, and wire fields, and convert at a checked boundary or use std::ssize.

reading.section: Promotions and the usual arithmetic conversions
reading.prompt: A permission byte has its low nibble cleared. What does this print?
reading.explain: `~low_nibble` promotes its operand to `int` before complementing, so it is `~15`, that is `-16` — the bit pattern 0xFFFFFFF0, not the eight-bit 0xF0. Comparing it with the `int` literal 240 is therefore false. The tempting reading is that a `std::uint8_t` operand keeps eight-bit arithmetic and both lines agree. The masking still produces the intended 0b1011_0000 = 176, because the extra one-bits above bit 7 are cut away when the `int` result converts back to `std::uint8_t` — the bug is only visible when the intermediate value is compared instead of stored.

reading.prompt: A sliding window reports how many more samples it can take. What does this print?
reading.explain: `window.size()` is `std::size_t`, whose rank is at least that of `int` on this platform, so the usual arithmetic conversions convert `capacity` to `std::size_t`. `4 - 10` is then computed modulo 2^64 and yields a huge positive value, which is greater than zero: the guard says there is room. The tempting reading is that both lines must agree because both spell the same subtraction. In `headroom` that same huge value is converted back to `int` on return, which since C++20 is the value congruent modulo 2^32 — a well-defined -6. One expression is a wrapped unsigned comparison, the other a wrapped-then-narrowed signed result.

reading.prompt: Three tenths of a second are accumulated one tick at a time. What does this print?
reading.explain: Neither `0.1` nor `0.3` is representable in binary64; each is stored as the nearest representable value. Summing the stored `0.1` three times under round-to-nearest lands one ULP above the stored `0.3`, so the equality is false and the ordered comparison is true. The tempting reading comes from the printed value: at one significant digit the sum formats as `0.3`, so the number *looks* equal to the constant it is being compared with. Printing is a rounding of the value, not the value.

reading.prompt: Exactly one of the three numbered lines is ill-formed. Which one, and why do the other two survive?
reading.explain: Line (3) is ill-formed: a scoped enumeration has no implicit conversion to an integer, and there is no built-in `operator|` taking `std::uint8_t` and `LogFlag`. Lines (1) and (2) compile because both name the conversion explicitly — `std::to_underlying` in one case and a `static_cast` in the other. The tempting reading is that the fixed underlying type `std::uint8_t` makes the enumeration interchangeable with that type; it fixes the *representation*, not the conversion rules. That is the whole point of `enum class`: bitmask arithmetic must be requested, either by converting at the boundary or by giving the type its own operators.

reading.prompt: A latency histogram builds a table of power-of-two bucket edges. Where does this program leave the language, and what does the standard say about the result?
reading.explain: At `i == 30` the multiplication computes 2^31, which is not representable in a 32-bit `int`. Signed overflow is undefined behaviour, so the program has no defined result at all — UBSan reports `signed integer overflow: 1073741824 * 2 cannot be represented in type 'int'`. The tempting reading is that the multiplication "wraps to INT_MIN" and the last edge simply prints as -2147483648; that is a description of one machine, not of the language, and an optimiser is entitled to assume the loop never reaches an overflowing iteration. Declaring `edge` as `unsigned` makes the wrap defined, and `std::int64_t` makes all 32 edges representable.

reading.prompt: Only one of these two functions compiles. Which one fails, and why does the other survive with the same-looking arithmetic?
reading.explain: `first_of_next_month` is ill-formed. `d.month + 1` promotes `d.month` to `int`, and converting an `int` *expression* back to `std::uint8_t` inside braces is a narrowing conversion, which brace initialization rejects. The literal `1` in the same braces is fine: it is a constant expression whose value the compiler can prove fits in `std::uint8_t`, and constant expressions that fit are exempt. `next_day` compiles because the `static_cast` states the narrowing explicitly. The tempting reading is that the compiler rejects the line because month 13 is out of range — it has no idea what a month is; it is objecting to the *type* of `d.month + 1`, and would object identically if the sum were provably 2.

reading.prompt: A stock-keeping routine tops up the emptier of two bins. What does this print?
reading.explain: A reference cannot be reseated. `emptiest = bin_b` is not a rebind; it is an assignment *through* the reference, so it writes 3 into `bin_a`. `emptiest` still names `bin_a`, and `+= 1` makes it 4, while `bin_b` is untouched at 3. The tempting reading — "`emptiest` now refers to `bin_b`, so the output is 7 4" — is exactly the Java/Python model of a name. To select an object at runtime you need a pointer (`int* emptiest = &bin_a; ... emptiest = &bin_b;`), or you must bind the reference in its initializer with a conditional expression.

reading.prompt: A ring buffer hands out slots two ways. What does this print?
reading.explain: `ring[i % ring.size()]` is an lvalue of type `int`, so `decltype(auto)` deduces `int&` and `slot` returns a reference into the vector: `slot(ring, 6)` names slot 2 and the assignment stores 42 there. Plain `auto` on the same expression drops the reference, so `slot_copy` returns a copy — and `auto taken = slot(...)` likewise copies, which is why writing 7 into `taken` leaves `ring[2]` at 42. The tempting reading is that `taken` aliases the slot because the function it was initialized from returns a reference; the declaration form of the *variable*, not the value category of its initializer, decides that.

writing.prompt: A log line arrives as `char line[64]`. Write `count_commas` twice: a two-pointer form `count_commas(begin, end)` in which the walking cursor may be advanced but never used to write, and the end pointer may never be advanced or used to write; and a one-argument overload taking the buffer itself that does not lose the bound to array-to-pointer decay. Neither overload may copy the buffer or use a C-style cast.
checklist: The walking cursor is declared `const char*` — reseatable, read-only pointee
The end parameter is declared `const char* const` — both the pointer and the pointee are const
The one-argument overload takes `const char (&line)[64]`, a reference to the array, not `const char line[64]`
That overload derives its end pointer from the bound rather than from a repeated literal 64 in the body
No `const_cast` or C-style cast appears
writing.notes: Read the declaration outward from the identifier: `cursor` is a pointer to const char, `end` is a const pointer to const char. A parameter written `const char line[64]` is adjusted to `const char*` and the 64 enforces nothing, which is why the second overload binds a reference to the array instead — the bound is part of the array type and survives.

writing.prompt: A tokenizer tags each token with a one-byte kind on the wire. Write a scoped enumeration `TokenKind` with a fixed underlying type covering Word, Number and Punct plus an Invalid state, and the pair of boundary functions `to_wire(TokenKind) -> std::uint8_t` and `from_wire(std::uint8_t) -> TokenKind`. `from_wire` must map every byte outside the declared set to `TokenKind::Invalid`; it must never produce a `TokenKind` value that no enumerator names.
checklist: `enum class TokenKind : std::uint8_t` — scoped, with an explicit underlying type
`to_wire` uses `std::to_underlying` (or a `static_cast`) rather than an implicit conversion
`from_wire` validates the incoming byte before producing an enumerator, and has a default/else path returning `Invalid`
No unchecked `static_cast<TokenKind>(byte)` on unvalidated input
writing.notes: A fixed underlying type means `static_cast<TokenKind>(200)` is a valid *value* of the type rather than undefined behaviour — it is still not a token kind your switch statements handle. The fixed type buys layout, not domain validation; the `default` arm buys the domain.

writing.prompt: Write `bool fits(std::size_t used, std::size_t capacity, std::size_t incoming)`, answering whether `incoming` more bytes fit in the buffer. The function must never evaluate an unsigned subtraction whose result could wrap, and must answer `false` rather than `true` when the caller passes a `used` that already exceeds `capacity`.
checklist: The over-capacity case is handled before any subtraction is performed
Exactly one subtraction appears, and it is guarded so that its left operand is not smaller than its right
The comparison is written against `capacity - used`, not as `used + incoming <= capacity` (which can overflow the sum)
The function has no signed/unsigned mixed comparison
writing.notes: The naive `used + incoming <= capacity` is wrong in the other direction: the sum can wrap past zero and make an enormous request look small. Subtraction is safe once you have proved the left operand is the larger; that proof is the `if`.

writing.prompt: A thermometer driver hands you a `double` in Celsius. Write `is_valid_reading(double)`, accepting only finite values in the closed range -60 to 85, and `to_decidegrees(double)`, converting a validated reading to tenths of a degree rounded to nearest (half away from zero), not truncated. Explain in a comment why a range check written only as `if (celsius > 85.0) return false;` is not sufficient.
checklist: Finiteness is tested with `std::isfinite` (or equivalent) *before* the range comparisons
Both ends of the range are checked, and the range test is inclusive
`to_decidegrees` rounds via `std::lround`/`std::round` rather than a bare `static_cast<int>`
A comment states that every ordered comparison with NaN is false, so a NaN passes an inverted check
writing.notes: `static_cast<int>(celsius * 10.0)` truncates toward zero, so 20.49 and 20.99 both become 204 — and a value the driver reports as 20.5 may be stored as 20.499999999999996. Rounding is a separate decision from converting.

writing.prompt: A decaying activity score is updated on every event. Write `double decay(double level, double factor)` that returns the decayed value, except that any result whose magnitude has fallen below the smallest positive *normal* double is returned as exactly `0.0`, so the loop can never enter the subnormal range. Add a compile-time check that the target actually uses IEEE 754 doubles.
checklist: `static_assert(std::numeric_limits<double>::is_iec559)` (or equivalent) appears at namespace scope
The threshold is `std::numeric_limits<double>::min()`, the smallest positive normal — not `::epsilon()` and not `::denorm_min()`
The magnitude is compared, so negative levels are handled too
The clamped return is a literal `0.0` rather than the tiny product
writing.notes: `numeric_limits<double>::min()` is the smallest positive normal value, not the smallest positive value — that is `denorm_min()`. Clamping here is a deliberate change to the numerical contract, chosen in one place, which is very different from switching on FTZ/DAZ or `-ffast-math` for a whole translation unit.

writing.prompt: Write a `constexpr` table of the twelve month lengths of a non-leap year, and `int day_of_year(int month, int day)` taking a 1-based month. The element count must be checked at compile time from the array itself rather than written as a literal in a second place, and the function must never index the table out of range for a month in 1..12.
checklist: The array is declared with a deduced bound (`constexpr int kMonthLength[] = {...}`)
A `static_assert` derives the count with `sizeof(table) / sizeof(table[0])` (or `std::size`) and checks it is 12
The 1-based month is converted to a 0-based index exactly once
The accumulation loop stops before the current month rather than including it
writing.notes: The `sizeof` idiom works only while the array type is in scope. Pass `kMonthLength` to a function declared `int f(int months[12])` and the parameter is a plain `int*`: `sizeof` then reports the pointer size and the compile-time count is gone.

writing.prompt: A C logging library calls back with `void* payload, std::size_t len`, and wants a `void* context` that you can only supply as a `const Config*`. Write the forwarding function using the narrowest named cast for each conversion — the payload viewed as `const char*`, the config passed as the context, and the payload address recorded as a `std::uintptr_t` identifier. One comment per cast naming the permission it requests. Then state, in a final comment, which cast becomes undefined behaviour depending on how the pointed-to object was created.
checklist: `static_cast` is used for `void*` to `const char*` (no `reinterpret_cast` there)
`const_cast` is used only to drop the `const` on the config pointer
`reinterpret_cast` is used only for the pointer-to-integer conversion
No C-style cast appears anywhere
A comment states that writing through the de-const-ed pointer is undefined if the `Config` object was itself created `const`
writing.notes: Each named cast advertises exactly one power, which is why they are greppable review points. A single `(char*)payload` would have performed the `static_cast` and quietly stood ready to strip `const` as well.

writing.prompt: Write two loops over a `std::vector<int>` used as a ring buffer: one that doubles every slot in place, and one that prints every slot without copying it. Add a commented-out third loop showing the spelling that compiles, runs, and silently changes nothing — with a comment naming the deduction rule responsible.
checklist: The mutating loop declares the variable `auto&`
The observing loop declares the variable `const auto&`
The commented-out loop uses plain `auto` and the comment says plain `auto` drops the reference and produces a copy
Neither live loop takes an index or calls `size()`
writing.notes: For an `int` the copy costs nothing and only the semantics differ, but the same rule applied to `std::vector<std::string>` turns an observing loop into a per-element allocation. Choose the declaration form deliberately even when the element is cheap.
